solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Solecism a no-no?

definitions.meaning: a grammatical blunder such as 'I didn't do nothing', where two denials cancel
read literally, 'no-no' is a pair of noes, two denials side by side

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a grammatical blunder is simply something to avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no-no' looks like slang for something forbidden; read literally it is two noes together, which is what the grammatical fault consists of.
explanation.definitionFit: Using two denials in one statement, as in 'I ain't got none', is a classic grammatical error frowned on by purists.

clue.text: Bob Tanner's inheritance?

parts.note: a bob was a shilling and a tanner a sixpence, pre-decimal British coins; read as a man's name, Bob Tanner inherits wealth from a long-established family

explanation.surface: A man called Bob Tanner wonders what he has been left in a will.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob (a shilling) and tanner (sixpence) are slang for coins of Britain's pre-1971 currency, so the 'name' is really a pair of obsolete coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Inherited family wealth of long standing is called this phrase, which also describes pre-decimal British coinage.

clue.text: US TV's top for ladies

definitions.meaning: American slang for the television set, the 's being 'is'
a tight strapless tube of stretchy fabric worn as a woman's top

explanation.surface: A claim about which American television programme ranks highest with women viewers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top' looks like 'best', but it is a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call a television this slangy name, and the same phrase names a strapless elasticated garment worn across the chest.

clue.text: Singularly abhorrent mortal

indicators.note: singularly means strangely or peculiarly, so the letters of the next word are arranged in an odd new way

explanation.surface: Someone is described as a uniquely detestable human being.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singularly' seems to intensify 'abhorrent', but it signals rearranging all nine of its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something born of the soil rather than the heavens is human and subject to death, the opposite of divine.

clue.text: See 1
More unfeeling, biting and calculating

parts.note: more numb, a comparative of numb meaning without feeling
chomping noisily into something

explanation.surface: A list of a cold person's traits: callous, sharp-tongued and scheming.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is not the word for a figure but 'numb' with -ER, meaning more lacking in sensation.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing large amounts of arithmetic or processing figures is informally described with this phrase.

clue.text: A number on dope discovered in port

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: a dope is a fool, a twerp

explanation.surface: Drugs found on board a ship in a harbour, perhaps a numbered consignment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dope' suggests drugs in the surface but means an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: This Belgian city on the Scheldt is one of Europe's largest seaports.

clue.text: Catholic queen needs investment warning — austerity's beginning!

parts.note: an ISA is a British Individual Savings Account, a tax-free investment
a bell rings as an alarm or warning

indicators.note: beginning means just the opening letter of the word austerity is taken

explanation.surface: A monarch is told to heed a financial alert at the start of belt-tightening.
explanation.walkthrough: An ISA is a tax-free savings account in the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella I of Castile, who with Ferdinand was given the title 'the Catholic Monarchs', is the queen meant.

clue.text: Arriving — or, as described, 'garrivin'?

definitions.meaning: finally reaching a place or state
the nonsense word is the word arriving with its last letter G taken to the top, which in a down entry is going up

explanation.surface: A dialect pronunciation of 'arriving' is offered as an alternative spelling.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, moving the final G of ARRIVING to the top gives 'garrivin': its ending has gone up.
explanation.definitionFit: To finish in a particular place or situation, often unexpectedly, is to arrive there.

clue.text: Incomplete concept leads to Mrs Leadbetter returning … it could be a hash!

indicators.note: incomplete means the word for concept loses its final letter

parts.note: a concept is an idea

indicators.note: returning means Margo's name is read backwards

parts.note: Margo Leadbetter is the snobbish neighbour in the British sitcom The Good Life

explanation.surface: A half-formed notion leads a sitcom character back home, perhaps in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hash' suggests a muddle or a stew; here it is the # sign. Margo Leadbetter is a character in the 1970s BBC sitcom The Good Life.
explanation.definitionFit: A symbol standing for an idea rather than a sound, like the # sign, is an example of this kind of written character.

clue.text: Bill's welcoming conjunction that's about to happen

indicators.note: welcoming means the word for bill takes the conjunction into its middle

parts.note: a bill is an advertisement, AD; the 's means 'is'
than is a conjunction used in comparisons

explanation.surface: A man called Bill greets a meeting that is imminent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a name but is an advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: Something close by in time, imminent or approaching, is described with this phrase.

clue.text: Son frequently going to Oxford, say, dancing

parts.note: oft is an old word for often
an Oxford is a style of laced leather shoe

explanation.surface: A son often travels to Oxford University to go dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford' looks like the university city but is a type of shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A style of tap performance done in soft-soled footwear without metal taps names this kind of dancing.

clue.text: Humble fellow lets one in

indicators.note: lets ... in means the word for fellow admits the next piece into its middle
with lets, in tells us the piece goes inside

parts.note: a dean is a senior fellow of a college
one, meaning the speaker, is me

explanation.surface: A modest man lets someone come inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humble' is a verb here: to lower in dignity.
explanation.definitionFit: To humble someone is to lower their standing or degrade them, a synonym.

clue.text: Chelsea perhaps joining party in reform centre

parts.note: a Chelsea boot is an ankle boot with elastic sides
a camp is a party or faction holding a view

explanation.surface: Chelsea football club, perhaps, joins a political party at a rehabilitation centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chelsea' suggests the London football club or district; it is a style of ankle boot.
explanation.definitionFit: A short, harsh, military-style detention centre for young offenders is a kind of correctional institution.

clue.text: Chap I briefly own up to in statement

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: briefly means the word for own up is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: to fess up is to own up, confess

explanation.surface: A man admits something in a formal statement.
explanation.definitionFit: A party's published declaration of its policies and aims is a public statement of intent.

clue.text: One picks it from hilly regions

indicators.note: from means the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone selects something from upland areas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picks' looks like choosing; it means plucking strings.
explanation.definitionFit: A small stringed instrument of ancient Greece was played by plucking, so a player picks it.

clue.text: Convicts about to lug up snails

indicators.note: about means the word for convicts goes round the other piece

parts.note: lags is British slang for convicts

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word for lug is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to lug is to drag

explanation.surface: Prisoners are about to haul up some snails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' looks like 'on the point of'; 'about' is the container signal and 'to' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Snails are proverbially slow, so slowcoaches who trail behind are figuratively called snails.

clue.text: So I hared off for the old country…

indicators.note: off means the letters have gone astray and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone ran off in a hurry, heading for the former homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hared off' reads as 'ran away'; 'off' alone signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The African state that is now Zimbabwe (and Zambia) bore this former name, so it is an old country.

clue.text: Cousin of 15's keen: 'Seconds out!'

definitions.note: a related stringed instrument to the one at 15 across; the 's is 'is'

indicators.note: out means the letter for seconds is removed

parts.note: keen means sharp, as of a blade

explanation.surface: A boxing referee's call, 'Seconds out!', is shouted keenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds out!' is the boxing call before a round, but here S (seconds) is taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are plucked stringed instruments, so a large triangular-framed one is a relative of the ancient Greek one.

clue.text: …where natives live in house with male antelope

parts.note: an eland is a large African antelope

explanation.surface: Continuing from 16, describes where locals live with a male antelope in their home.
explanation.definitionFit: The country one is native to is the place people born there inhabit.

clue.text: Ruminants held sway 'ereabouts, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means the words are as they would be spoken

parts.note: held sway is reigned, and 'ere is here with the H dropped, as in Cockney speech

explanation.surface: A dialect speaker says some animals once dominated the area near here.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the H of 'here', as many British accents do, gives 'ere; 'reigned 'ere' then sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: These cud-chewing deer of the Arctic are ruminants, like cattle and sheep.

clue.text: Implication of union agitating to embrace objective

indicators.note: to embrace means the shuffled letters go round the next piece
agitating means the letters of union are stirred up into a new order

parts.note: an end is an aim or objective

explanation.surface: A trade union's campaign hints at its true goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'agitating' fits a trade union's activism but turns union into INNUO, which then embraces END.
explanation.definitionFit: A sly hint or indirect suggestion, often insulting or risqué, is an implication.

clue.text: Singleton and I had to support hip patient

indicators.note: in a down entry a supporting piece sits below, so the others come first

parts.note: hip and in both mean fashionable
Valerie Singleton was a presenter of the BBC children's programme Blue Peter
I'd is a contraction of I had

explanation.surface: A single person and the speaker help someone with a hip complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singleton' suggests a single person but is the TV presenter Valerie Singleton. 'hip patient' looks like orthopaedics.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ill or disabled under care is a patient, the noun sense.

clue.text: Turn by female lead — she was barely supported!

parts.note: a go is a turn, as in a game
a diva is a leading female singer

explanation.surface: A performance by a leading lady who wore very little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barely' means naked: Lady Godiva rode through Coventry unclothed on a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says this noblewoman rode naked on horseback through Coventry, so her mount held her up while she was nude.

clue.text: A very loud, funny niece about to provide reviver

indicators.note: about means the reordered letters go round the other pieces
funny means the letters of niece are made strange, reordered

parts.note: FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A noisy, comical niece is about to hand someone a pick-me-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funny' rearranges NIECE to CEINE, which goes 'about' A and FF.
explanation.definitionFit: The stimulant in coffee perks people up, so it is a reviver.

clue.text: Take a steer in mostly corroded limousine with no innards

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter of the word for corroded

parts.note: corroded metal is rusty

indicators.note: with no innards means only the outermost letters remain

explanation.surface: Someone takes the wheel in a rusting limousine with its insides gutted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'steer' suggests driving; it is a bullock. A Limousin is also a cattle breed, adding to the farmyard cover.
explanation.definitionFit: To steal livestock such as a bullock is a cattle thief's crime.

clue.text: How to move the earth, beyond doubt!

definitions.meaning: an idiom meaning to a great degree, emphatically

explanation.surface: Moving the earth is, without question, possible.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom meaning in large measure, emphatically, also literally describes digging with garden tools.

clue.text: Gerrup! On yer feet! Them's regulations!

definitions.meaning: commands to get up from sitting, instructions to rise
permanent rules governing proceedings, such as those of a parliament

explanation.surface: A sergeant bawls at recruits to rise, insisting those are the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the phrase means instructions to get up; in the usual sense it means the fixed rules of a body.
explanation.definitionFit: A parliament's or society's permanent procedural rules are called by this phrase, which also suits commands to rise.
